11.quote_or_event: “At the end of duḥṣamāduḥṣamā in utsarpiṇī, there will be five clouds that will rain for seven days each. Among these the first, named Puṣkara will sow the earth; the second, named Kṣīramegha, will make grain spring up; the third, Ghṛtamegha, will produce oil; the fourth, Amṛtamegha, will make herbs, et cetera.”
11.explanation: In Jain cosmology, when the worst age of the time-cycle ends, a series of great rains, including an 'amrita-cloud', restores the ruined earth and makes life possible again.
11.tie_back: Jain tradition, too, imagines world-renewing rain as amrita, the nectar that brings the dead world back to life, which is just what the Kural calls rain.
11.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book X (Mahaviracharitra), ch. XIII, 'Utsarpini' (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
11._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; a vivid parallel, but in Jainism these rains come from the impersonal turning of the time-cycle, not as a divine gift, and the passage concerns cosmic renewal rather than everyday rainfall.

12.quote_or_event: “There are beings living in water, many lives; of a truth, to the monks water has been declared to be living matter.”
12.explanation: Jainism counts water itself as a body of one-sensed souls (apkaya), so monks strain or boil their drinking water and limit its use to avoid harming those lives.
12.tie_back: Where the Kural celebrates rain as both the maker of food and food itself, Jainism adds a distinctive ethical note: the very drink rain provides is alive and must be used with restraint.
12.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1.3.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
12._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; next-best match only, since the Jain text turns the Kural's praise of rain-as-drink into a caution about harming water-beings rather than a celebration.

13.quote_or_event: Digambara tradition holds that a twelve-year famine in north India drove the teacher Bhadrabahu to lead an exodus of monks south to Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, joined, the tradition says, by Chandragupta Maurya, the first Mauryan king, who had become a Jain monk.
13.explanation: In Digambara memory a famine scattered the whole monastic community and moved Jainism south. Some scholars treat the migration as the start of the Digambara–Svetambara split, and Svetambara accounts instead send Bhadrabahu to Nepal.
13.tie_back: It is a Jain memory of just what the Kural warns: when the rains fail, hunger seizes the land and overturns even the life of a religious order.
13.source: Bhadrabahu–Chandragupta famine-migration tradition (Digambara), as summarised in Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bhadrabahu I'
13._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from a reputable encyclopedia. I could not consult the Shravanabelagola inscriptions directly (archive.org rate-limited me). The story is a sectarian tradition whose dating and details are historically disputed, and it shows famine's effects rather than teaching anything about rain.

14.quote_or_event: “The husbandmen throw the corn on high ground and on low ground, hoping (for a return). For the like motive give unto me; I may be the field which may produce merit (as the return for your benevolence).”
14.explanation: The Jain monk Harikesha, refused alms at a Brahmin sacrifice, appeals to the farmer's hope of a harvest to show that giving to a self-controlled ascetic is a field that yields merit.
14.tie_back: It draws on the same farming life the Kural describes, in which ploughing and sowing are acts of hope in a return, though the Jain verse uses farming as a metaphor rather than speaking of drought.
14._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; next-best match, since the shared ground is the farmer's dependence on a return, not the failure of rain that stops the plough.

15.quote_or_event: “Then the clouds will be without water. Clouds of acid and clouds of vinegar, clouds of poison, fire, and lightning will rain what is similar to themselves.”
15.explanation: Jain cosmology pictures the worst age ending with destructive rains that ruin fields, forests, and grass, after which the five nourishing clouds of the next age bring the earth back to life.
15.tie_back: This two-sided picture of rain that first lays the world waste and then raises it again closely mirrors the Kural's claim that rain both ruins and restores.
15.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book X (Mahaviracharitra), ch. XIII, 'The sixth spoke' (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
15._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong structural fit of destroying and restoring rain, though on a cosmic time-scale rather than the seasonal flood and drought the Kural has in mind.

16.quote_or_event: “'For in the rainy season living beings, grass, seeds, mildew, and sprouts frequently come forth.'”
16.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra's rules for the monsoon retreat tell monks to inspect the ground with special care in the rains, because that is when grass and countless small lives spring up everywhere.
16.tie_back: It confirms from the Jain side the Kural's observation that grass appears only when rain falls, and for Jains each such blade is itself a living, one-sensed soul to be protected.
16.source: Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis §55 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
16._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close observational match, framed in Jainism as a reason for non-harm rather than as praise of rain.

17.quote_or_event: “The function of the souls (jīva) is to help one another.”
17.explanation: Umasvati's sutra, parasparopagraho jivanam, became the motto of Jainism: living beings exist in a web of mutual support and mutual dependence.
17.tie_back: The Kural's sea that shrinks when the cloud stops giving back illustrates the same principle of reciprocity: what is taken must be returned, or even the greatest reserve declines.
17._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; next-best match, since the sutra concerns souls aiding one another, while the Kural's sea and cloud are not souls in that sense, and no Jain text found treats evaporation and rain this way.

18.quote_or_event: “In that period, in that age the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra commenced the Paggusan when a month and twenty nights of the rainy season had elapsed.”
18.explanation: Paryushana (here Paggusan), the most important annual Jain festival of fasting, confession, and scripture-reading, is fixed by the rainy season, when monks stay in one place and lay people gather around them.
18.tie_back: As the Kural says, the great festivals and regular worship depend on the rains, and the chief Jain festival is literally timed by the monsoon.
18.source: Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis §1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
18._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Jacobi's 'Pa-g-g-usan' rendered as Paggusan); partial fit, since Jains do not offer worship to celestials for rain, and this ties festival to the rainy season rather than to the rain's success or failure.

19.quote_or_event: “At that moment the gods caused a rain of perfumed water and flowers, and showered down heavenly treasures; they struck the drums, and in the air they praised the gift.”
19.explanation: When the outcaste-born monk Harikesha, after fasting a whole month, finally receives alms, the gods rain down perfumed water and treasure to honour both the gift and the austerity.
19.tie_back: The story joins exactly the Kural's pair, dana (the gift) and tapas (the month-long fast), and marks their meeting with a rain from the sky.
19._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it pairs giving and austerity with rain, but the causality is reversed, with rain as the gods' response to virtue rather than its precondition.

20.quote_or_event: “In the morning there will be destruction of right-conduct; at mid-day, of kingly duty; in the afternoon, of fire.”
20.explanation: Hemacandra's account of the coming age of pure sorrow links the collapse of right conduct with a world where 'the clouds will be without water', so moral and natural order fail together.
20.tie_back: Like the Kural's pun on ozhukku as both flowing water and right conduct, the Jain picture treats the failure of rain and the failure of conduct as one decline.
20.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book X (Mahaviracharitra), ch. XIII, 'The sixth spoke' (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
20._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; partial fit, since in Jain cosmology both are effects of the declining time-cycle rather than conduct depending on rain, and the same chapter supplies Kural 15's entry.
